title: Applications of DBMS
summary: Discover how Banking, Airlines, E-Commerce, Healthcare, Universities, and Telecom rely on DBMS daily.
definition_text: DBMS powers almost every modern digital domain—including Banking & Finance (transfers, ledgers), Airlines (real-time seat reservations), Universities (courses & transcripts), E-Commerce (inventory & orders), Healthcare (EHRs), and Telecommunications (call & billing logs).
example_text: When you buy the last concert ticket online, the e-commerce DBMS locks that inventory row so nobody else can purchase the same ticket.

title: SQL EXISTS
summary: Test efficiently whether a correlated subquery returns at least one matching row using EXISTS.
definition_text: EXISTS Operator: a Boolean predicate that is TRUE when its subquery returns at least one row and FALSE when it returns none. The optimizer may stop once it has enough information, but performance relative to IN depends on the query plan and data.
example_text: Listing customers who have placed at least one order in 2026. Example: SELECT d.dept_name FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects p WHERE p.dept_id = d.dept_id);

title: SQL UNIQUE Constraint
summary: Prevent duplicate values in columns like email or course_code using UNIQUE.
definition_text: UNIQUE Constraint: Constraint ensuring all values in a column or column group are distinct across rows. The `UNIQUE` constraint prevents duplicate key values in a column or column combination. NULL handling for UNIQUE constraints varies across database engines; in SQLite, multiple NULL values are allowed. A table can define multiple UNIQUE constraints, unlike its single PRIMARY KEY constraint.
example_text: Enforcing unique `course_code` (`CS301`) and unique `email` in `students`. Example: SELECT student_id, email FROM students;

title: SQL CREATE INDEX
summary: Create a secondary search structure that may speed up suitable lookups and joins.
definition_text: CREATE INDEX: DDL command creating a search structure on table columns that a query planner may use for suitable operations. `CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table_name(column_name);` builds an index, commonly a B-tree, on the selected column. An index may reduce work for suitable `WHERE`, `JOIN`, or `ORDER BY` operations, but the query planner and workload determine whether it is used. Indexes require storage and must be maintained during writes.
example_text: An index on `students(dept_id)` may reduce the work for a selective department filter; confirm use with the engine’s query-plan tools. Example: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM students WHERE student_id = 3;
